scenes.tts: Most sensory receptors are excited by their stimulus. Vertebrate photoreceptors are turned off by theirs. A rod sitting in the dark is depolarized. Current flows steadily into it, and it releases glutamate all the time. Light makes it stop. How does turning a cell off let you see?
scenes.visual: A rod with glutamate dots streaming up into a question-mark box and blue current flowing in; a light arrow arrives and the stream stops.
scenes.narration: Most sensory receptors are excited by their stimulus. Vertebrate photoreceptors are turned off by theirs. A rod sitting in the dark is depolarized. Current flows steadily into it, and it releases glutamate all the time. Light makes it stop. How does turning a cell off let you see?

scenes.tts: In darkness, cyclic G M P holds C N G channels open in the outer segment. Sodium and calcium flow in. That steady dark current keeps the rod depolarized, so it releases glutamate. Now a photon is absorbed by rhodopsin. One activated rhodopsin activates many transducins. Transducin activates P D E six, which breaks down cyclic G M P. The channels close, and the dark current shrinks. The rod hyperpolarizes, and glutamate release falls.
scenes.caption: In darkness, cGMP holds CNG channels open in the outer segment. Sodium and calcium flow in. That steady dark current keeps the rod depolarized, so it releases glutamate. Now a photon is absorbed by rhodopsin. One activated rhodopsin activates many transducins. Transducin activates PDE6, which breaks down cGMP. The channels close, and the dark current shrinks. The rod hyperpolarizes, and glutamate release falls.
scenes.visual: Outer-segment membrane with open CNG channels held by cGMP; a photon reaches rhodopsin, transducins and PDE6 appear, cGMP vanishes, channels close, inflow stops, release meter falls.
scenes.narration: In darkness, cGMP holds CNG channels open in the outer segment. Sodium and calcium flow in. That steady dark current keeps the rod depolarized, so it releases glutamate. Now a photon is absorbed by rhodopsin. One activated rhodopsin activates many transducins. Transducin activates PDE6, which breaks down cGMP. The channels close, and the dark current shrinks. The rod hyperpolarizes, and glutamate release falls.

scenes.tts: The rod releases one transmitter, glutamate. It releases more in the dark and less in the light. Yet some bipolar cells depolarize to light, and others hyperpolarize. Glutamate's sign is set by the receptor, not by the molecule. OFF bipolar cells use AMPA or kainate receptors. In the dark, glutamate opens cation channels and depolarizes them. Light removes that excitation, so they hyperpolarize. The sign is preserved.
scenes.visual: Rod feeds two bipolar cells; one goes up and one goes down in light; the OFF cell shows its AMPA or kainate channel opening in the dark and closing in light, with a sketch trace dipping.
scenes.narration: The rod releases one transmitter, glutamate. It releases more in the dark and less in the light. Yet some bipolar cells depolarize to light, and others hyperpolarize. Glutamate's sign is set by the receptor, not by the molecule. OFF bipolar cells use AMPA or kainate receptors. In the dark, glutamate opens cation channels and depolarizes them. Light removes that excitation, so they hyperpolarize. The sign is preserved.

scenes.tts: ON bipolar cells use a different receptor, m G L U R six. In the dark, glutamate on m G L U R six activates the G protein Go. Go keeps the channel T R P M one closed. Light lowers glutamate. Go activity declines, and T R P M one opens. The cell depolarizes. The sign is inverted.
scenes.caption: ON bipolar cells use a different receptor, mGluR6. In the dark, glutamate on mGluR6 activates the G protein Go. Go keeps the channel TRPM1 closed. Light lowers glutamate. Go activity declines, and TRPM1 opens. The cell depolarizes. The sign is inverted.
scenes.visual: ON bipolar cell: mGluR6 to Go, a blocking arrow onto closed TRPM1; in light the chain dims and TRPM1 opens; a sketch trace rises opposite to the OFF trace.
scenes.narration: ON bipolar cells use a different receptor, mGluR6. In the dark, glutamate on mGluR6 activates the G protein Go. Go keeps the channel TRPM1 closed. Light lowers glutamate. Go activity declines, and TRPM1 opens. The cell depolarizes. The sign is inverted.

scenes.tts: So each photoreceptor feeds two parallel streams, one signalling lighter and one signalling darker. ON bipolar cells drive ON ganglion cells. OFF bipolar cells drive OFF ganglion cells. In cat retina, light on the centre of a field makes an ON centre ganglion cell fire faster, and suppresses an OFF centre cell. Ganglion cells fire action potentials. They are the retina's only output.
scenes.visual: Circuit boxes: photoreceptor to ON and OFF bipolar to ON and OFF ganglion cells with typed arrows, then sketch spike trains: ON speeds up and OFF falls silent when light falls on the centre.
scenes.narration: So each photoreceptor feeds two parallel streams, one signalling lighter and one signalling darker. ON bipolar cells drive ON ganglion cells. OFF bipolar cells drive OFF ganglion cells. In cat retina, light on the centre of a field makes an ON centre ganglion cell fire faster, and suppresses an OFF centre cell. Ganglion cells fire action potentials. They are the retina's only output.

scenes.tts: Light switches the photoreceptor off, and the retina reads that silence in two opposite ways. OFF bipolar cells keep the sign. ON bipolar cells invert it. Keep this rule. The receptor, not the molecule, sets the sign.
scenes.visual: One glutamate stream splits into the OFF keeps-sign and ON inverts-sign readers; the rule is written under them.
